title: Self-Programmed Execution for Language-Model Agents
claim: Existing agents keep orchestration in a fixed harness loop; ours lets the model's own program be the orchestrator.
layout: 3 panels side-by-side, top-to-bottom flow, color-coded boxes inside dashed runtime box
description: Three vertical flow diagrams sit side by side, titled (a) ReAct, (b) RLM and (c) SPE. Each starts with a grey Input box at the top and ends with a grey Output box at the bottom, joined by arrows. A dashed rounded rectangle labeled 'harness runtime' encloses the core logic. In (a) and (b), a blue 'Harness code' box (maintains state, builds prefix, calls LM) sits above a yellow box, 'Model instructions' in (a) and 'Model code' in (b). A feedback arrow loops from the yellow box back to the blue box. In (c) there is only one tall yellow 'Model code' box listing state, prefix, LM calls, tools, subagents and halting, with a self-loop arrow. The blue shrinks and then disappears from left to right, which draws the eye to the all-yellow panel (c).
caption: Three agent architectures. Colored boxes distinguish program logic that is implemented in the harness (blue) vs. written by the model (yellow). In all cases, these programs are executed by a harness runtime which is external to the model. (a) In ReAct [Yao et al., 2023], the model selects from a prescribed action space. An orchestrator program runs the agent loop, maintaining state (e.g., conversation history) across turns. (b) Recursive language models (RLMs) [Zhang et al., 2026] execute model-written orchestration code inside a harness-managed main-agent loop, which performs handoff between the main agent’s own turns. (c) In SPE, a model-written program specifies the orchestration policy, free of any outer agent loop. The model-written program is still executed by an external runtime.
abstract: At the heart of a language model agent is an orchestrator program which is responsible for the state transition between consecutive turns. In existing systems, this program is implemented in the harness. This paper introduces self-programmed execution (SPE), in which the model completion is itself the orchestrator program, and the harness evaluates this program but does not impose any fixed orchestration policy. Formally, an SPE state of an agentic machine is one from which a model completion can load any successor state up to an embedding, and an instance of an SPE state is one which executes the model completion as a program. In practice, the program requires a language with unusual features, as its source code doubles as the content of the model's context window. I therefore introduce Spell, a Lisp dialect in which programs can edit and re-evaluate themselves, and effectful expressions like model invocations are structured such that re-evaluating an edited program does not replay its side effects. Experiments with existing models, not trained for SPE or Spell, show that frontier models can learn Spell in-context and accomplish challenging agentic tasks. These results demonstrate how an LM can act as an agent without any fixed orchestration policy, and they raise the question of what self-orchestration strategies might be learned by a model trained for self-programmed execution. Code is available at https://github.com/lukejoconnor/spell.
